summary:
Salta Province stands under Argentina's national framework. Law 26.743 was approved by the Chamber of Deputies 167-17-7 and by the Senate on 9 May 2012 by 55 votes to one abstention, promulgated on 24 May 2012, and permits a change of legal gender without surgery, without hormone treatment and without judicial approval. The United Nations described the statute as a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region. Argentina was the first Latin American country to legalise marriage equality, in 2010, and anti-discrimination protection exists through a combination of national and provincial laws.

Trans people in the country have had an 'X' option on the national identity document since 2021, and that marker remains part of the formal legal position alongside the 2012 statute. Trans activists interviewed in April 2025 reported that the law is still formally in force but is no longer guaranteed in practice, pointing to administrative and budgetary measures rather than to any repeal.

Executive action has narrowed the framework. A decree of 5 February 2025 issued by the government of President Javier Milei restricts minors' access to gender-affirming surgery and hormone therapy, and a second decree governs the housing of transgender people in prisons. Legal experts called the decree on minors illegal and unconstitutional and petitioned the courts to intervene; the outcome of that litigation is not recorded in the sources available here.

The same government eliminated the national Ministry of Women, Gender and Diversity and dismissed trans public servants hired under the federal Trans Labor Quota Law, which reserves 1% of public-sector posts for trans people. Activists say the quota is no longer being implemented, which removes an employment protection that trans residents, including those in Salta, would otherwise rely on.

Violence against LGBTIQ+ people reached a documented high in 2025. The national hate-crime observatory recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity during the year, a rise of 62% year-on-year and the worst figure in the observatory's ten years, averaging one every 38 hours. Agencia Presentes reported the figures on 19 March 2026.

Trans women and travestis accounted for 62.5% of victims, 142 of the 227 cases. Physical attacks on bodily integrity made up 64.8% of cases, 147 in total, with beatings the main modality. Perpetrators were predominantly security-force personnel and unidentified attackers in public space, and the observatory attributed the surge to the government's 'cultural battle' and its hate discourse. The same period saw the decree of February 2025 restricting minors' gender-affirming treatment.

Protection machinery has weakened at the level of individual cases. On 5 April 2025 Argentina's Supreme Court left standing the life sentence imposed on Gabriel Marino for the 2015 murder of trans activist Diana Sacayán, but rejected attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance removed by an appeal court in 2020, so the gender-motivated-crime aggravator does not apply in the case as it now stands.
tangentialFactors:
Trans activists in Buenos Aires interviewed on 4 April 2025 by the Washington Blade, including representatives of organisations named for Diana Sacayán, stabbed to death in 2015, and for Lohana Berkins, said the Milei government's policies had made the community more vulnerable to violence and described the situation as chaotic and desperate. Their testimony concerns the capital rather than Salta, but it reflects a national policy direction that reaches every province.

An Outright International country overview updated on 12 March 2026 records negative assessments on same-sex relations, on gender recognition and on organisation registration, indicating deterioration against the country's earlier position as a regional leader on LGBTIQ+ rights. The country was the first in Latin America to legalise marriage equality, in 2010, which makes the direction of travel rather than any single measure the notable comparison.

The removal of the travesticidio aggravating circumstance in the Sacayán case on 5 April 2025 leaves a life sentence intact but strips the gender-motivated element from the judgment, a signal about how hate-motivation is treated by the higher courts even as recorded hate crime runs at a record level.
localsOnly:
Residents of Salta Province access legal gender change directly through the national registry under Law 26.743, without surgery, hormone treatment or a court order, and the 'X' marker has been available on the national identity document since 2021.

The federal Trans Labor Quota Law reserves 1% of public-sector posts for trans people. Activists report that the trans hires made under it have been dismissed and that the quota is no longer being implemented, so residents who relied on that route to public employment have lost it in practice while the statute remains on the books.

The elimination of the national Ministry of Women, Gender and Diversity removed the dedicated federal body that had handled gender and diversity policy, including referral and support functions that provincial services in Salta would have leaned on.

For trans minors in Salta the decree of 5 February 2025 restricts access to gender-affirming surgery and hormone therapy, and the separate decree on prisons governs where transgender detainees are held. Both bind residents directly regardless of what the 2012 statute says.

Provincial anti-discrimination law operates alongside the national statutes, giving residents a provincial complaint route in addition to federal remedies.
outOfScopeNotes:
The litigation challenging the February 2025 decree on minors as illegal and unconstitutional has no recorded outcome in the sources available here; whether the restriction stands or has been stayed is unresolved.

It is not sourced whether the Trans Labor Quota Law has been formally repealed or simply not enforced; activists describe non-implementation, and no regulatory act withdrawing it appears in the inventory.

No Salta-specific evidence on enforcement, police conduct, access to facilities or provincial services is present in this inventory. The violence figures are national, and the observations about ministry closure and quota dismissal come from interviews with activists in Buenos Aires, so their application to Salta rests on the national reach of those measures rather than on local documentation.

Whether the national government's 'cultural battle' framing, cited by the observatory as an driver of the 2025 violence surge, has been adopted or resisted by Salta provincial authorities is not sourced.
